Ms. Robin Lee Moore, age 74, of Wildwood, Florida died Saturday, July 25, 2026, at her daughter’s home in Jacksonville, Florida following an extended illness. She was born in Swainsboro, Georgia on November 23, 1951, and was a was 1970 Graduate of Lyons High School. She enjoyed ballroom dancing, karaoke, and cooking. She is preceded in death by her father, Robert L. Moore, Sr., 1972; mother, Iris Wiggins Moore 2023; and brother, Robert L.” Bob” Moore, Jr., 2025 She is survived by three children, Kelly Evans and husband Harold of Jacksonville, Florida, John Moore Jr. and wife Mary Dawn of Lyons, Georgia, Michael Griggers and Wife Christina of Atlanta, Georgia; six grandchildren, Lindsey Brock, Joey Bushnell, Maura Moore, Mattie Moore, Rayna Toole, and Sherwood Griggers; four great-grandchildren, Brycen Brock, Jace Brock, Cohen McCoy, and Kashton Moxley. She will be forever remembered for her kind heart, vibrant spirit, and the unconditional love she so generously shared with her family, friends, and all whose lives she touched. Her compassion, strength, and selfless devotion will remain a lasting source of comfort, and her memory will be cherished with love in our hearts forever. The family will receive friends at the funeral home on Saturday afternoon, August 1, 2026, from 1:00 until 3:00 with a family graveside funeral service to follow at Mt. content: Only 3 items found for keyword as Yu-Gi-Oh%20Legendary%20Arc-V%20Decks%20TCG%20Sealed%20Box, categoryId as 261044 and in the region EBAY-US we can’t display the banner right now. ARC-V built its whole story around the idea that every summoning mechanic deserved its own dimension, and Konami is cashing that premise in one more time. Legendary Arc-V Decks reach Official Tournament Stores on August 5 and general retail on August 7 at an MSRP of $31.99 per box. Inside are three complete, ready to play decks pulled from three dimensions, including Odd-Eyes for Yuya out of the Standard Dimension, Lunalight for Celina out of the Fusion Dimension, and Speedroid for Yugo out of the Synchro Dimension. The structure mirrors March’s Legendary Modern Decks 2026 exactly. Each Deck runs 55 cards, split into a 40-card Main Deck and a 15-card Extra Deck, and each carries one Secret Rare plus six Ultra Rares. Every Deck also ships with a bonus pack holding a 56th card, a Secret Rare copy of one of six eligible cards from that Deck, with a chance to upgrade to a Starlight Rare instead. Total contents come to 168 cards: three Secret Rares, 18 Ultra Rares, 144 Commons, and the three bonus Secret Rares. *Buy Yu-Gi-OhI Legendary Arc-V Decks on TCGPlayer or eBay Yuya’s Deck gets the headline new card plus a long-awaited import. Odd-Eyes Override Dragon is the Link-3 LIGHT Dragon with 2500 ATK that Konami teased first. It destroys another card you control to draw, and if that card was a Pendulum Monster Card, you get an extra Pendulum Summon for your Performapal, Magician, and Odd-Eyes monsters. It also negates an opposing effect during your turn by discarding a card. Alongside it, Odd-Eyes Solblaze Dragon finally crosses to the West. This Level 8 Synchro Tuner debuted in Japan as an OCG Structures promo in October 2024 and has never seen an English printing until now. Performapal Skullcrobat Joker takes the Secret Rare slot, and the Extra Deck brings an alternate art Accesscode Talker at Ultra Rare, plus Chaos Angel, I:P Masquerena, and S:P Little Knight. Lunalight finished as runner up at the 2025 World Championship, so this Deck needed less help than the other two. It gets it anyway. Lunalight Scarlet Tiger is a Level 5 DARK Beast Warrior that Special Summons itself from hand whenever a Lunalight monster’s effect goes off, and if your opponent has already acted that turn, it fetches Polymerization from your Deck or Graveyard. Brotherhood of the Fire Fist – Tiger King is the Secret Rare, a natural fit for an archetype built on Beast Warriors and running three copies of Fire Formation – Tenki. Pot of Prosperity, Crossout Designator, Triple Tactics Talent, and Triple Tactics Thrust round out a genuinely modern support shell. Yugo’s build leans on Speedroid Darumaknocker, a Level 4 WIND Machine Tuner that Special Summons itself from hand by sending a Speedroid card from your Deck to the Graveyard, locking you into WIND monsters for the turn. Send it from the field to the Graveyard and it searches a Speedroid Spell or Trap, then destroys a monster on the field if you control a Clear Wing monster. Crystal Clear Wing Over Synchro Dragon takes the Secret Rare slot. The six Ultra Rares cover Speedroid Terrortop, Speedroid Taketomborg, Darumaknocker itself, Hi-Speedroid Kitedrake, Hi-Speedroid Glider #2, and Hi-Speedroid Rubber Band Shooter. *Buy Speedroid Terrortop cards on TCGPlayer or eBay Add the three Decks together and the hand trap suite is substantial. You get three copies of Ash Blossom & Joyous Spring, three Called by the Grave, three Infinite Impermanence, four Droll & Lock Bird, two Nibiru, the Primal Being, two Effect Veiler, and one each of Mulcharmy Fuwalos, Mulcharmy Meowls, and Mulcharmy Purulia. Worth being clear-eyed about what that means. Legendary Modern Decks 2026 already dumped a wave of Common rarity staples into the market back in March, and this box does it again. That is excellent news if you are assembling a competitive Deck on a budget, and steady downward pressure if you have been sitting on Common printings waiting for them to appreciate. *Buy Ash Blossom & Joyous Spring cards on TCGPlayer or eBay Eighteen cards are eligible for the bonus pack Secret Rare treatment, six per Deck, and each can upgrade to a Starlight Rare instead. The Odd-Eyes candidates include Performapal Monkeyboard, Sky Iris, and Beyond the Pendulum. Lunalight offers Lunalight Black Sheep, Lunalight Scarlet Tiger, and Lunalight Liger Dancer, among others. This is the second product to use what Konami informally calls Starlight 2.0, following Chaos Origins. The adjustments produce richer color and swap the old grey outer border for a rainbow foil one, which reads most dramatically on extended art cards. *Buy Odd-Eyes Solblaze Dragon cards on TCGPlayer or eBay Parker Johnson is an accomplished journalist and content writer with nearly nine years of experience. title: The V-8 sports sedan that blends Lexus reliability with real pace - How-To Geek
content: Performance sedans rarely deliver everything in one package. German rivals offer incredible speed and technology but can become expensive to own over time, while many Japanese alternatives prioritize reliability at the expense of outright excitement. The Lexus IS 500 takes a different approach. By pairing a naturally aspirated V-8 with rear-wheel drive and Lexus' reputation for long-term dependability, it offers a combination that has become increasingly rare in today's market. For enthusiasts who want genuine performance without worrying about long-term ownership, the IS 500 stands out as one of the last sports sedans to blend old-school character with everyday reliability. To give you the most up-to-date and accurate information possible, the data used to compile this article was sourced from Lexus and other authoritative sources, including Classic.com, CarMax, Edmunds, and TopSpeed. Lexus leads the pack when it comes to reliability, making many of their models a great choice for buying used. Today's sports sedans are faster, more refined, and more technologically advanced than ever before. But for buyers planning to keep one beyond its warranty period, outright performance is only part of the equation. German models such as the Audi S4 continue to set the benchmark for all-round capability, combining turbocharged power, all-wheel drive, and premium interiors. However, that performance can come with higher maintenance and repair costs as mileage increases. Japanese luxury brands have traditionally taken the opposite approach. Models from Lexus and Acura are known for their durability and lower running costs, but many have historically lacked the level of performance and driver engagement enthusiasts expect from a true sports sedan. A rare sports sedan that pairs performance with real long-term trust. Performance cars built around naturally aspirated V-8 engines are becoming increasingly uncommon. As manufacturers adopt smaller turbocharged engines and hybrid powertrains to meet stricter emissions regulations, Lexus has remained committed to a more traditional formula with the IS 500. That formula traces its roots back to the original IS F, introduced for the 2008 model year. Its Yamaha-developed 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V-8 quickly earned a reputation as one of the finest Japanese performance engines ever produced, combining high-revving character with exceptional durability. Today, that same engine lives on in the IS 500 F Sport Performance. It makes the Lexus one of the last rear-wheel-drive luxury sedans to offer naturally aspirated V-8 power, giving it a character that few modern rivals can replicate. Old-school performance in a world full of forced induction. The heart of the IS 500 is its 5.0-liter naturally aspirated 2UR-GSE V-8, producing 472 horsepower and 395 lb-ft of torque. With a 7,300-rpm redline, it delivers the kind of linear power delivery and unmistakable soundtrack that has become increasingly rare in modern performance cars. The engine is about more than outright performance. Yamaha-designed cylinder heads, titanium intake valves, dual D-4S fuel injection, forged internal components, and a generous oil capacity all contribute to a design that has earned a reputation for long-term durability as well as impressive performance. Despite lacking turbochargers or all-wheel drive, the IS 500 remains genuinely quick. Lexus quotes a 0–60 mph time of around 4.3 seconds, putting it firmly in the company of established German sports sedans while retaining the simplicity of a naturally aspirated V-8. It’s fast, refined, and packed with features. This Japanese sports sedan proves performance doesn’t have to cost a fortune. The IS 500's appeal goes beyond its engine. Lexus paired the V-8 with an Aisin eight-speed automatic transmission that has earned a reputation for strength and long-term dependability, favouring durability over the razor-sharp shift speeds of some dual-clutch gearboxes. That philosophy extends throughout the car. Rather than chasing the latest performance technology, Lexus focused on proven engineering that can withstand years of enthusiastic driving without the higher maintenance costs often associated with more complex European rivals. For buyers planning to keep a performance sedan for the long haul, that matters just as much as outright speed. The IS 500 offers the kind of mechanical simplicity that has become increasingly difficult to find in today's luxury sports sedan market. These are the Toyota and Lexus models that take on the world’s most luxurious automakers, delivering unmatched style, performance, and comfort. The IS 500 is just as comfortable commuting through traffic as it is tackling a winding back road. Its well-insulated cabin, supportive seats, and adaptive suspension give it the refinement expected of a modern Lexus, while the naturally aspirated V-8 transforms the experience at the press of the accelerator. Fuel economy is the biggest compromise, but that is hardly surprising for a high-revving 5.0-liter V-8. Buyers considering the IS 500 are far more likely to value its character and performance than chase the lowest fuel bill. That character is what makes the car so memorable. The combination of the V-8's induction noise, the exhaust note, rear-wheel drive, and predictable handling creates an experience that few modern sports sedans can match, regardless of price. Here are 10 used high-performance luxury sedans that offer unmatched power, precision, and value—outshining even newer, more expensive rivals. Our sister site, TopSpeed, recently spent time behind the wheel of the Lexus IS 500 F Sport Performance and came away impressed by how cohesive the package feels. The review praised everything from the seating position and chassis balance to the naturally aspirated V-8, describing it as one of the few modern sports sedans that feels genuinely analogue. On the road, the IS 500 stood out for its direct steering, controlled body movements, and strong braking performance. The limited-slip differential and linear power delivery made it rewarding to drive on twisty roads, while the lack of turbochargers meant smooth, uninterrupted acceleration all the way to the engine's lofty redline. The cabin also left a lasting impression. TopSpeed highlighted the excellent sound insulation, high build quality, and everyday comfort, concluding that the IS 500 asks very little of its owner while delivering an experience that few German or Japanese rivals can now match. If you're after long-term dependability without giving up luxury, these pre-owned sedans stand out for their proven reliability and lasting quality. The IS 500 held an MSRP of roughly $61,000 to $67,000 when new, but the used market is beginning to make it far more attainable. Recent sales show well-kept examples changing hands for noticeably less, with higher-mileage cars offering particularly strong value. That demand has also helped the IS 500 retain its appeal. Many examples on the market have covered relatively few miles, suggesting owners are holding onto them rather than trading them in after a few years. For enthusiasts, that creates an interesting opportunity. Buying used can put one of the last naturally aspirated V-8 sports sedans within reach, while still benefiting from Lexus' reputation for long-term durability. These are 10 Japanese luxury cars renowned for their performance design, and exceptional craftsmanship. The Lexus IS 500 offers something increasingly difficult to find in today's performance car market. It combines naturally aspirated V-8 power, rear-wheel drive, and proven mechanical durability in a package that remains comfortable enough to use every day. While rivals may offer more technology or quicker gear changes, few deliver the same combination of character and long-term confidence. The IS 500 stays true to a formula that many manufacturers have already abandoned, making it feel special every time you get behind the wheel. For buyers looking beyond outright performance figures, the IS 500 is one of the most compelling sports sedans available. It proves you don't have to sacrifice reliability to enjoy an engaging, high-performance driving experience. We want to hear from you. title: The V-10 Engine May Be Gone, But These Cars Will Never Be Forgotten - Road & Track
content: We love a good V-10 engine, and these are the best of the bunch. New production cars that use V-10 power are no more. That train left with the departure of the Lamborghini Huracán and the Audi R8, which means this list is full of greatest hits from the past. Many are supercars, but there’s the occasional odd duck in the mix, too, including a few oddball SUVs and pickup trucks. These are the best V-10-powered cars ever made. The Viper may be dead now, but it’s the car we think of first when it comes to legendary, V-10-powered machines. The track-ready ACR version is a beast on the circuit, with a big 645-hp 8.4-liter V-10 and comically large aero. Prices for the ultra-barebones first-gen are still within reason, but the fifth-gen has skyrocketed in value since the Viper went out of production. No matter which version of the Lamborghini Huracán you prefer, you're getting a naturally aspirated 5.2-liter V-10 that shrieks its way to a high redline. This mid-engine Lamborghini has talents that span from the racetrack with the STO to excellence off-road with the Sterrato. Its successor, the hybrid Temerario, loses two cylinders and tacks on a couple of turbochargers. The Audi R8 was initially offered with a V-8, but not long after launching, it added a 5.2-liter V-10. Throughout its long production run, the R8 tended to follow the Lamborghini Huracán. We finally saw Audi’s incredible supercar go out of production after 2023 production concluded, but just like Lamborghini, Audi has a twin-turbo V-8 successor with its Nuvolari. Before the Huracán, the Gallardo held court as the entry-level Lambo supercar. This angular, mid-engine success story produced 493 horsepower and matured across 10 model years, birthing dozens of iterations and special editions. They’re still not cheap, but you can pick one up at the bottom of the market for around the $100,000 mark today. Read our 20-year retrospective review of the Gallardo The Porsche Carrera GT is one of the most special Porsches ever produced. You can trace its engine’s lineage back to Le Mans and F1 cars, which the sound should remind you of instantly. The 5.7-liter V-10 paired with a manual transmission is a combination for the ages, one its 918 successor even struggled to compete against. This particular Porsche is one of the greatest sports cars ever made in addition to being one of the greatest V-10s. WHY THE CARRERA GT IS STILL PORSCHE'S GREATEST SUPERCAR The LFA makes a strong argument for being the best-sounding car of all time. Lexus teamed up with Yamaha's musical instrument division, and they tuned the LFA's engine note like it was a guitar. Described by Toyota engineers as a "roar of an angel," we agree wholeheartedly. The 553 horsepower seems almost secondary. Almost. The LFA name is being revived for an EV to come in the future, but we’ll never forget this V-10 masterpiece. The E60-generation BMW M5 is perhaps one of the scarier used-car purchases one can make today, but that doesn’t make it any less tempting. Bellowing up to a redline of 8250 rpm, the 5.0-liter, F1-inspired V-10 in this M5 produced 500 horsepower and 380 lb-ft of torque. Its subtle and classy exterior makes this V-10-powered super sedan one hell of a sleeper. The M5 wasn't the only BMW M car to receive that magnificent 5.0-liter V-10. The big-boy, two-door M6 got the same engine, paired to either a seven-speed single-clutch automated manual or a traditional six-speed. Both are sure to cost you dearly to maintain, but it’s hard to complain too much after listening to its incredible soundtrack. In keeping the German super-sedan theme going, we present the Audi S8. It uses a 5.2-liter Lamborghini-related V-10 to haul its 4300-pound body to 60 mph in 4.8 seconds. The tuxedo-trim good looks and everyday usability made this car an excellent balance between work and play. If it wasn’t clear by now, you can tell the VW Group made good use of its V-10 from this era. The only pickup truck on this list is a banger. This is the Dodge Ram SRT-10, a two-door Ram with a wing and a gargantuan 8.3-liter naturally aspirated V-10 borrowed from the Viper. You could even get it with a manual transmission. It remains the ultimate performance truck to this day, but Ram is coming for its own crown with the Hellcat-powered Rumblebee launching next year. How cool is a diesel-powered V-10? Cool enough for U.S. emissions regulations to cancel the Touareg TDI's sales here (twice). Twin turbos aid the ten cylinders, and the engine produces 310 horsepower and 553 lb-ft of torque. Besides this Volkswagen, the only other V-10-powered SUV made was the Ford Excursion, making it an extremely rare breed. VW IS MULLING A NEW FLAGSHIP SUV FOR A MORE AFFLUENT CROWD The McLaren Solus GT is the by far the newest V-10-powered car on this list. It's a track-only special with a unique 5.2-liter engine that revs to 10,000 rpm and has 829 horsepower and 479 lb-ft of torque. Thanks to its slim single-seater design and carbon fiber monocoque, it weighs just 2205 pounds. It’s an absolute rocketship. title: SUV Comparison: 2026 Toyota RAV4 Woodland vs Honda CR-V Hybrid Trailsport - driving.ca
content: This pair of hybrid crossovers took a peek at Subaru’s notes—and copied them to differing degrees of success You can save this article by registering for free here. Or sign-in if you have an account. It’s an enlightened world, this 2026. For so long, Subarus were just out there. At last, however, others are finding their way from the shadows to shed their chrome and embrace a tougher truth — or at least try a little on for size. So arrive the 2026 Toyota RAV4 Woodland and Honda CR-V Trailsport. Each taking their brands’ small hybrid crossovers for a walk on the wild side while retaining the core practicalities they’re regarded for, these lightly ruggedized new trims commit to different lengths: one with decision, the other a Demi Lovato, as it were. Both the 2026 RAV4 and CR-V have reached their sixth generations, the Toyota graduating this year while the Honda debuted four years back. Unsurprisingly, then, there’s a little more spring to the RAV4 than the CR-V: fresher in style and technology, the Toyota is distinctly more modern on approach and inside. Toyota’s strong and straightforward new-gen infotainment system has been updated, with a few tweaks to settings and menus. The Honda CR-V’s native infotainment, on the other hand, felt somewhat rudimentary and dated even at launch — moreso after these few years, not to mention in comparison to the Toyota RAV4’s. In either case of course, most drivers will likely spend most of their time in either car’s standard wireless Apple CarPlay or Android Auto interfaces. Around this, too, the RAV4’s interior feels a touch more interesting: pleasant, soft-textured vinyl upholsters all trims above base; soft-touch synthetic panels line the doors and dash; and a few thoughtful cubbies around the interior make for a more versatile space. The CR-V remains more straightforward in both materials and layout: even the CR-V’s soft-ish surfaces feel plasticky and uninspiring by comparison, if still durable and functional in the easy-wipe ride-share sense. Lower CR-V trims (this Trailsport included) aren’t helped by Honda’s cheap-feeling cloth-seat upholstery; this alone may be enough funnel some shoppers toward more expensive trims. Much closely aligns between the two from here on: point here, point there. Both SUVs received matching IIHS safety ratings of 5.0, with eight airbags in the Toyota and 10 in the Honda CR-V. Highway wind noise is better isolated in the Toyota, but both models’ Ontario assembly lines — Toyota’s world-leading Cambridge plant, in particular — are known for well-buttoned output. Passenger space is too similar to note in most measures, the biggest differences being the CR-V’s advantages of an inch of rear headroom and three inches’ more leg and hip room. The RAV4 wins on seats-up cargo volume with 1,070 litres (42 L more), while the CR-V measures 53 L more at 2,030 litres with seats folded. Note that the RAV4’s hybrid battery is packaged under the rear seats to accommodate a spare wheel under the trunk floor, contributing to an imperfect cargo floor with seats folded. The Honda’s hybrid battery occupies the space under its trunk floor, crowding out any underfloor storage but freeing the rear seat bottoms to collapse downward for a flatter fold than the Toyota. Along with that lower ride height, this makes the CR-V the friendlier ute to load cargo into. Perhaps more important than those touch points is the models’ hybridization. The 2026 Toyota RAV4 is a hybrid as standard, while the 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid is a higher grade above a base gas-only powertrain. We’ll discuss pricing in more detail later, but the critical detail here: the $39,430 base 2026 Toyota RAV4 hybrid prices near the non-hybrid CR-V, but the 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid models don’t start until way up at $47,900. Power is something of a toss-up between the two, both making correct figures for the segment. The Honda is less powerful, yet feels lighter and quicker on its feet than the Toyota. It’s unexpectedly pleasant to accelerate either mildly or hurriedly, and the CR-V’s handling around curves and ramps is more engaging while the RAV4 feels a smidge bulky to manoeuvre. The new RAV4’s 2.5-litre four-cylinder engine pairs with a conventional ‘parallel’ hybrid motor for 236 horsepower and 242 pound-feet of torque. A 1.59-kWh hybrid battery can run the car short distances at low speeds before the engine kicks on. The CR-V Hybrid employs a 2.0-litre four, pairing with its hybrid motor for 204 hp and 247 lb-ft. This powertrain generally achieves the smoother, quieter drive thanks to Honda’s unique ‘two-motor’ hybrid arrangement: one drives the car, the other is driven by the engine as a generator. The CR-V Hybrid’s gas engine only connects to the wheels through its ‘e-CVT’ (continuously variable transmission) at higher loads and speeds; it otherwise primarily serves as a sort of range extender to charge the 1.04-kWh battery while the electric drive motor handles low-speed duties, where it’s the more powerful and efficient partner. Yet for all the Honda’s cleverness, the Toyota RAV4 is the better hybrid. Not only is the RAV4’s hybrid power a standard feature and less expensive than the CR-V’s, it’s also more efficient on paper and as tested across similar routes and conditions. NRCan consumption ratings for the 2026 Toyota RAV4 Woodland are 5.7 L/100 km city, 6.7 L/100 km highway, and 6.2 L/100 km combined; I observed an even better 6.0L/100 km average. NRCan consumption ratings for the 2026 Honda CR-V Trailsport are 6.3 L/100 km city, 7.2 L/100 km highway, and 6.7 L/100 km combined; I observed 6.7L/100 km. The Toyota RAV4 grows into this identity as well as could be hoped, adopting trail-adjacent attire if not to the serious degree of Toyota’s truckier TRD Off-Road models. It’s starting from a different place, of course, but here, as in the previous gen’s latter-years’ Woodland trims, there seems a commitment to make a meaningful effort within the bounds of the everyday practicality still expected of the model. The 2026 RAV4 Woodland’s larger ‘all-terrain’ tires afford it an extra centimetre of ground clearance — enough to count without throwing accessibility, handling, or highway efficiency out the window. Grille-mounted LED fog lamps offer more illumination for nights in the forest, and crossbars span its roof rails for canoes or other overhead cargo. Most importantly, the Woodland is the one trim to fit a trailer hitch as standard. The Honda CR-V’s Trailsport treatment is a halfhearted foray. Mounting similar ‘all-terrain’ rubber but riding at the same height as usual, the Trailsport is somewhat thinly distinguished even as an outlier trim package. Highlights include orange accent lighting, badging, and trim pieces. A “silver skid garnish” mimics the appearance of underbody protection, but you’re not going to want to catch it on any nasty obstacles. It’s a flavour-of-the-moment costume without conviction. Still, one point to Honda, here: the CR-V Trailsport gets a dedicated low-speed traction mode for more challenging surfaces. Neither of these crossovers’ all-terrain tires are destined for much past the trailhead, of course: though treadier than the usual all-seasons for modest terrain beyond the tarmac, these light-duty tires match the cars’ suitability for mild campgrounds and cottage tracks. This isn’t a knock, though: proper off-road tires are noisy and unpleasant to live with. For vehicles designed and destined to spend most of their lives in town and commute, this sensible compromise is no disappointment. The base 2026 Toyota RAV4 hybrid prices from $39,430 after destination ($455 more than the base CR-V), but the 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid models start way up at $47,900. In fairness to Honda, however, a base price is just what gets feet in the door: shop a mid-range volume trim with more popular options and the gap quickly narrows. The two hybrids tested here list quite close to one another at $48,930 for the 2026 Toyota RAV4 Woodland; and $49,300 for the 2026 Honda CR-V Trailsport. Though similarly priced, these rugged trims are positioned differently within their respective hierarchies. The Honda Trailsport represents the first small step up from the respectably equipped (Hybrid) base; the Toyota Woodland is a more substantial upgrade from base ‘LE’ and volume-trim ‘XLE’ that most shoppers will likely look toward. In either case, these trims’ creep toward $50k also reminds of their proximity to the larger (if less efficient) Subaru Outback that we tested here. The Outback is also new for 2026, and (unfortunately for existing fans) has grown into an outright SUV with a larger, more versatile cargo area and passenger cabin than either the RAV4 or the CR-V. Importantly, too, Subaru has discarded its unpleasant old infotainment in favour of a licensed version of the Toyota system seen here. For perspective, however, the Outback’s economy is more conventional, with NRCan ratings of 9.3 L/100 km city, 7.5 highway, and 8.5 L/100 km combined. Other competitors in the segment include the Hyundai Tucson Hybrid from $44,845 and platform-sibling Kia Sportage Hybrid from $43,545. Hyundai-Kia products continue to offer strong value propositions, squeezing in more line-item feature content per dollar to entice buyers who aren’t so keen to pay the ‘Toyota Tax.’ NRCan-reported economy figures for these hybrids run 6.7 L/100 km in all categories for the Hyundai, and low 6’s for the Kia. The Mazda CX-50 Hybrid is offered from $45,145. Higher trims offer classy, properly premium cabin appointments — though most buyers will trim a level or two shy of those more glamorous, caramel-upholstered specs. Economy ratings are posted between the RAV4 and CR-V Hybrids at 6.1 L/100 km city, 6.4 highway, and 6.2 combined. Both the 2026 Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V Hybrid offer strong, Ontario-built hybrid buys. The CR-V’s older design remains respectable, with an innovative and effective hybrid system and a livelier drive that spares it quite the appliance-like on-road character of the RAV4. Appliance is the brief, however, and the alternative offered by Toyota is generally more appealing for a comparable spend. These outdoorsy trims — or at least Toyota’s — bring a little flair to the appliance practicality, of course, a worthwhile consideration whether or not you’re hauling Blundstones and harnesses. Still, neither of these trims should be understood as go-tos within their lineups: our picks are the entry 2026 CR-V Sport Hybrid ($47,900) and the 2026 RAV4 XLE ($43,230). That first Hybrid CR-V trim fits most of the core-priority content including heated steering wheel, wireless mobile charging and projection, power liftgate, and power (albeit underwhelmingly textured cloth) seats; that second-up RAV4 matches this list and adds that Toyota’s pleasant vinyl upholstery. As evident, the 2026 Toyota RAV4 distinguishes itself in both style and function. Even beyond its slight economy advantage, the RAV4’s friendlier physical and infotainment controls, versatile cabin storage, and general character give the ever-important sense that there’s ‘more vehicle’ there for the money. And of the Subaru-inspired garnishes at hand, Toyota’s more credible execution only further cements its case. (Then again: you could just shop an actual Subaru.) Korean pop group BTS has opted out of 2027 Grammys contention in apparent reaction to the awards’ newly created Best Asian Pop Music Performance category. “We have decided not to submit to the Grammys this year,” the boy band’s seven members — RM, Jin, Suga, J-Hope, Jimin, V and Jungkook — posted simultaneously, in Korean, on their respective Instagram accounts Wednesday. “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language. BTS, shorthand for the Bangtan Boys, is the acronym for the group’s official name, Bangtan Sonyeondan, or “Bulletproof Boy Scouts” in English. After a four-year hiatus to pursue solo projects and fulfill mandatory military service, BTS roared back with the March 2026 release of “Arirang.” The group is currently on its 85-show Arirang World Tour and will play to sellout crowds at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium Saturday and Sunday, where they memorably performed in the World Cup 2026 Final halftime show on July 19. BTS has been nominated for numerous Grammy awards over the years. “Arirang” was predicted to be an Album of the Year contender, with nods also expected for its lead single “Swim,” according to Deadline. The new Best Asian Pop Music Performance award is one of five new categories the Recording Academy unveiled last month. It “recognizes artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including but not limited to K-pop, J-pop and C-pop, with meaningful use of one or more Asian languages,” the Recording Academy said in a statement. In small communities, a social media post can travel fast. When that post accuses someone of dishonesty, theft or misuse of public funds, the legal consequences can be serious. Municipal governments in small centres often involve people who know each other personally, professionally and socially, and that closeness can make online accusations especially damaging when public debate crosses the line into defamation. A Saskatchewan court recently awarded $150,000 in damages plus interest from November 9, 2020, to June 16, 2026, after defamatory Facebook posts accused a former rural municipality administrator of lying, misallocating funds and theft. In Parry v. Harper, 2026 SKKB 113, the Court found that statements made about Ms. Parry, the former administrator of the Rural Municipality of Pleasantdale, Saskatchewan, were defamatory and caused significant reputational harm. In October and November 2020, Mr. Harper made comments on a Facebook page called “2016 Election R.M. 398” accusing Ms. Parry of lying, misallocating funds and theft. To prove defamation, Ms. Parry had to establish: The evidence showed that the words were communicated to people in Ms. Parry’s community. Others shared and commented on the Facebook posts, and Mr. Harper arranged for the posts to be sent to administrators in nearby municipalities. People also approached Ms. Parry in the community to discuss the posts. These findings were crucial to the Court’s damages award: the posts were not simply rude or critical – they directly attacked her integrity in a role that required public trust. The Court also considered that the posts remained online for years, were shared and discussed in the community and caused Ms. Parry humiliation, anxiety and reputational harm. For those reasons, the Court awarded $125,000 in general damages, plus $25,000 in aggravated damages because of Mr. Harper’s malice, the continued publication of the posts until the March 2026 trial date and his refusal to remove or justify the statements. In small communities, it is important to understand the difference between criticism and defamatory comments. Criticism of administrators and community leadership is acceptable, but not when it crosses the line into false allegations of dishonesty, theft, misuse of public funds or other misconduct. This case is a reminder that social media posts are not consequence-free, particularly where the comments are made in a close-knit community and concern a person whose role depends on public trust. Although this decision involved a rural municipality, the same principles can apply in other local governance settings, including urban municipalities, Indigenous communities and governments, Métis organizations and other community-based bodies. In all of these settings, public debate and political criticism have an important role, but serious online allegations should be grounded in facts and made with care because of the real reputational harm they can cause. title: Florida’s East Coast v. West. Which beaches are better to surf, swim? - Florida Today
content: The Sunshine State is famous for its beaches, boasting more than 1,300 miles of coastline and 825 miles of beaches, but no two beaches are the same. Among Florida's bounty of beaches, there's something for everybody. There are beaches with sugary sand, beaches with surf so calm it resembles a swimming pool, beaches that are great for finding seashells and shark teeth, beaches popular with spring break partiers, beaches that are great for dog walking, secluded beaches... the list goes on. There are even clothing-optional beaches for those who like to enjoy the sun and surf in the nude. Most longtime Floridians have a favorite beach, and some are territorial about what makes it the best beach. But if you're looking to take a Florida beach trip before the summer ends, the best beach for you depends on what you're looking for. While one side of Florida generally has calmer and more consistently clear blue or teal water, Florida's other coast has better surfing overall. Here's which side of Florida has better swimming beaches, which has better surfing beaches and lists of the best beaches in Florida for swimming and surfing. Although you can paddle out and catch a wave all around the state, Florida's East Coast has better, more consistent opportunities for good surf. The Atlantic side of the peninsula benefits more regularly from wind swells and produces more well-defined waves, due to its myriad of jetties and piers. "Florida encapsulates the East Coast surf scene unlike any other Atlantic State..." Stormrider Surf Guides says. "Despite the absence of regular groundswell and sizeable wave challenges, the average Florida surf can range from 1ft windchop to 20ft faces in a hurricane swell. Once again, it is the man-made structures that provide the best line-ups, sprinkled along both coasts." After all, 11-time World Surf League champion and professional surfing GOAT Kelly Slater grew up on Florida's East Coast waves. "Hawaiian, Californian and Australian surfers still scratch their heads in wonder at how Florida managed to produce Kelly Slater, the greatest surfer who ever lived, as well as a disproportionate number of athletes who earned spots on the elite world tour," Visit Florida's guide to the best beaches for surfing. "Most of Florida’s East Coast and some places along the Gulf offer a diversity of waves that have groomed some of the sport’s finest. Plus, the surf gets really good here in the Sunshine State, more often than you’d think, especially along the Treasure Coast." Summer isn't the best season for surfing in Florida, but many impatient local surfers waiting for the Atlantic Hurricane Season to peak and throw major swells to Florida's East Coast will paddle out anyway. "Traditionally, May through July is the flattest time of year; however, with a longboard and a good attitude, you can catch a lot of early morning sessions," Surfline says. "Still, there are no guarantees in summer, and when — or if — the next knee-high relief will arise is a mystery." The best season for surfing in Florida is in the fall, when tropical storm systems churning offshore in August and September bring in surf and are followed by cold fronts that send swells from the north by late October. On the West side of the peninsula, the Gulf of Mexico's waters are usually calmer, clearer, shallower and warmer. Many compare swimming in the Gulf to swimming in a giant (very salty) pool or lake. "Gulf Coast beaches have some of the most comfortable year-round water temperatures. The average water temperature in the summer months will range from about 82 degrees in Destin in June to almost 87 degrees in Tampa in August," Visit Florida says. "From the crook of Northwest Florida to the Dry Tortugas, the calm west coast seas attract everyone from sunbathers to shell hunters to spring breakers to scuba divers and everything in between. Even manatees and other finicky forms of sea life are drawn to Gulf Coast beaches and their warm, silky waters and quiet shorelines." As mentioned above, Florida's Gulf Coast waters are much better suited to swimming if you're looking for calmer, warmer waters. title: The People v. ICE's Cruelty - American Civil Liberties Union
content: With immigrant rights, trans justice, reproductive freedom, and more at risk, we’re in courts and communities across the country to protect everyone’s rights — and we need you with us. Your contribution to the ACLU will ensure we have the resources to protect people's rights and defend our democracy. Thanks for your support! Sign up to be the first to hear about how to take action. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails and text messages per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. Federal law enforcement have abused and terrorized countless people. We must demand justice for their victims. on behalf of people who’ve been harmed by the Trump administration’s violent and lawless practices and counting taking legal action to hold federal immigration agents accountable seeking justice for harm inflicted by federal law enforcement In recent weeks ICE has killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, following the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good in Minneapolis. Dozens more people have died in ICE's detention centers. Federal law enforcement are committing civil rights violations at a scale without precedent in our nation’s recent history, and with the support of an administration that encourages violence and disregard for the law. ACLU affiliates are fighting back by filing 54 claims across 17 states and Washington, D.C. against the federal government to demand justice for citizens and noncitizens alike who have suffered serious violence, abuse, and neglect at the hands of federal agents. Each claim tells an individual story. And together, they reveal a widespread pattern of civil rights violations and abuses that endanger us all. Check below to see where these claims have been filed and the types of abuses federal law enforcement has inflicted on our clients. Each case tells an individual story. And together, they reveal a widespread pattern of civil rights violations and abuses that endanger us all. Click each state to learn more about the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) cases filed. Sign up to be the first to hear about how to take action. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails and text messages per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. Federal law enforcement are abusing people who are simply exercising their First Amendment rights. Since the President Trump began his second term, people, regardless of their immigration status, have faced relentless attacks for exercising their First Amendment rights. 13 of our affiliates’ clients were retaliated against for exercising their First Amendment rights across 5 states and Washington, D.C. The ACLU of New Jersey’s client was operating a mobile health clinic outside an ICE detention center where active protests were taking place inside and outside the facility — then she was attacked by ICE. Norma Bowe, is a grandmother, professor of public health at Kean University, and registered nurse who operates a mobile clinic that provides free medical services to people across northern New Jersey. Since May 2025, her clinic has regularly stationed at Delaney Hall to support families visiting loved ones in the detention center. “ICE agents are acting like they have impunity and are inflicting harm however and whenever they want; without accountability, more people will get hurt and die. ICE must be held responsible.” - Dr. Norma Bowe Throughout the protests related to the detainees’ hunger strike, she was operating her mobile health clinic. One day, an ICE agent grabbed Norma and violently threw her to the ground. ICE is incarcerating people in dangerous facilities, where people detained are subjected to systematic abuse and egregious medical neglect. Right now, there are a record 65,000+ people in ICE detention facilities nationwide as the Trump administration rushes to expand the ICE detention machine fueled by the for-profit private prison industry. For decades, ICE detention has been notorious for horrific rights violations, medical abuse, and utter disregard for the dignity of people in custody. 14 of our affiliates’ clients experienced abuses in ICE detention, and their stories are only the tip of the iceberg. Two of the ACLU of Louisiana’s clients were denied access to medication, forced into physical labor, subject to severe physical and sexual abuse, and retaliated against, including by being placed in solitary confinement. Mario Garcia-Valenzuela and Luis Renteria Gonzalez were detained for nearly two and three years, respectively, at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. They suffered forced labor, physical abuse, sexual abuse, inadequate medical care, and severe retaliation by the facility’s staff, including placement in solitary confinement. “I’m speaking out now because ICE needs to be held accountable for what happened to me. And because I don't want this to happen to anyone else.” - Luis Renteria-Gonzalez As trans men, Mario and Luis were forced to perform intense manual labor in an off-the-books program that targeted transgender and masculine-presenting LGBTQ+ detained people. They were assaulted by officers and suffered serious injuries from forced labor. When Luis and Mario filed complaints about this abuse, they were held in solitary confinement for weeks, where they were denied food and access to their attorney. Mario was repeatedly denied his seizure medication, causing him to have at least 10 seizures in a one-month period, leading to his hospitalization. They both also experienced and witnessed sexual assault and harassment, including being forced to stand guard while an officer raped a detained woman. And when their families came to visit them in detention, officers stalked their families in the nearby town. ICE and federal law enforcement are racially profiling and arresting U.S. citizens unlawfully. Federal agents’ actions have not only harmed people without permanent legal status, but also U.S. citizens. In fact, more than half of our affiliates’ clients (29) were U.S. citizens harmed by federal law enforcement — and of those, 12 U.S. citizen clients were racially profiled and unlawfully detained. One of the ACLU of North Carolina’s clients, a U.S. citizen, was racially profiled and put into a unmarked SUV before federal agents released him, bleeding, on the side of the road. Willy Wender Aceituno, a U.S. citizen in North Carolina, was on his way into a restaurant when four armed and masked immigration agents surrounded him, pushed him against an agency’s vehicle, and forced him to provide identification to confirm his citizenship. Mr. Aceituno provided his Real ID driver’s license, and after confirming his citizenship, the agents walked away. But moments later after returning to his truck, agency vehicles pulled in front and behind him to block his exit. While he began to record, the agents shattered his window and attempted to grab his phone before holding Mr. Aceituno in a headlock and pulling him from his truck. He was thrown onto the pavement, which was covered in broken glass, and he suffered bleeding cuts all over his body. Mr. Aceituno was handcuffed, placed in an unmarked SUV, and driven away from the scene. He kept repeating that he was a citizen while the agents continued to tell him to “shut up.” Eventually, the SUV stopped, an agent took Mr. Aceituno’s wallet from his front pocket and confirmed that he was a citizen with no criminal record. The agents released Mr. Aceituno on the side of the road, still bleeding and 2 miles away from his truck. As these stories show, federal agents’ abuses are not limited to any one population, demographic, or surge. The ACLU’s new report, Agents of Chaos and Cruelty, underscores how federal agents' conduct has harmed citizens and noncitizens alike in states across the country. The report examines immigration enforcement incidents in eight states and found that over 400 of the more than 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents examined involved misconduct by immigration agents. Though the incidents examined represent a small fraction of total reported enforcement activity in 2025, the pattern across eight states makes clear that excessive force, racial profiling, intimidation, and abuse by both federal officials and state and local law enforcement are paramount to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant agenda.

title: Magnachip licenses Navitas’s GeneSiC silicon carbide technology for 1,200 V and above - Charged EVs
content: Posted July 29, 2026 by Chris Ruoff & filed under Newswire, The Tech. Magnachip Semiconductor is moving into the high-voltage and ultra-high-voltage silicon carbide market by licensing Navitas Semiconductor’s GeneSiC technology. The license covers Navitas’ Gen 4 and Gen 5 GeneSiC Trench-Assisted Planar (TAP) technologies at 1,200 V, 2,300 V, 3,300 V and higher. GeneSiC came to Navitas through its August 2022 acquisition of GeneSiC Semiconductor. Charged covered the Gen 5 platform when Navitas introduced it in February 2026. The TAP structure is the basis of Navitas’s high-voltage SiC devices for medium-voltage grid and infrastructure applications. Magnachip also gains access to Navitas’s SiC supply chain and materials ecosystem. The technology is planned to be ported, qualified and internalized at Magnachip’s fab in South Korea, and the companies expect that approach to speed Magnachip’s entry into SiC while maintaining continuity with Navitas’ existing technology and materials base. The companies say the licensed technologies will support applications including energy and grid infrastructure, energy storage, industrial electrification, automotive and other high-power systems in Korea. Navitas and Magnachip say the agreement also covers areas beyond SiC that they expect to detail later. “By licensing our proven GeneSiC technologies and supporting Magnachip through our supply-chain and materials ecosystem, we are creating a path to scale advanced SiC solutions more rapidly while enabling a deeper, long-term collaboration between our companies,” said Chris Allexandre, Navitas President and CEO. At 3,300 V and above, SiC devices compete with silicon IGBTs in grid-scale converters and traction drives. A higher blocking voltage per device reduces the number of parts that have to be connected in series, and SiC’s lower switching losses allow higher switching frequencies and smaller magnetics. “This agreement opens an important new market opportunity for Magnachip in high-voltage and ultra-high-voltage SiC,” said Chae Lee, Magnachip’s Chief Executive Officer. “The addition of GeneSiC technology complements our existing MOSFET and power semiconductor portfolio and positions Magnachip to serve customers that require higher efficiency, higher voltage capability and more reliable power conversion solutions.” The free webinar sessions from our Spring Virtual Conference are now available to view on-demand. title: The V-12 Is Nearly Dead — The Maybach S680 Is One Of The Last Cars You Can Actually Buy With One - Top Speed
content: Road & Track published its test of the 2027 Mercedes-Maybach S680, and the headline underneath the headline is harder to ignore than the car itself: a twin-turbocharged 6.0-liter V-12 still powers this thing, in 2026, available to order right now. That makes the S680 one of a shrinking handful of production cars where you can actually tick a V-12 on the options sheet and receive one. The engine format is not dead yet, but the obituaries are already being drafted. Lamborghini's Aventador successor, the Revuelto, pairs its V-12 with a hybrid system — a concession to emissions regulators that signals where even the most committed twelve-cylinder brands are heading. Rolls-Royce, Ferrari, and a small cluster of ultra-luxury and hypercar builders still offer the configuration, but confirmed phase-out timelines are tightening. If owning a V-12 production car matters to you, the window is measurably narrower than it was three years ago. The S680 rides on the Mercedes-Benz S-Class platform and tops the Maybach sedan lineup above the V-8-powered S580. Its 6.0-liter biturbo V-12 produces 621 horsepower and 738 lb-ft of torque, channeled through a nine-speed automatic to the rear wheels. Road & Track's verdict, published this afternoon, frames it plainly: nobody needs a V-12, but the S680 makes a compelling case for still wanting one. Base pricing for the 2027 S680 sits north of $240,000 in the United States. That's a significant premium over the S580, which Road & Track separately noted is good enough that buyers with a tight grip on their billions might reasonably skip the twelve. The S680's case rests almost entirely on the engine itself — its refinement, its torque delivery, and the particular kind of silence it produces at highway speeds that no V-8, however well-tuned, quite replicates. The confirmed list of V-12 production cars available to buyers today is short. Rolls-Royce fits every model it sells — the Ghost, Spectre excepted as an EV, the Phantom, the Cullinan, and the Dawn — with a 6.75-liter twin-turbo V-12 producing 563 to 591 horsepower depending on specification. Phantom pricing starts around $460,000; Cullinan Black Badge editions push well past $400,000. Rolls-Royce has not announced a phase-out date for the V-12, though the Spectre's existence signals the brand's electric direction. Lamborghini's Revuelto, the Aventador's replacement, keeps the naturally aspirated 6.5-liter V-12 but hybridizes it — three electric motors combine with the combustion engine for a combined 1,001 horsepower. Purists debate whether a hybridized V-12 counts as the real article; the combustion component is genuine, but the character is altered. Base price is approximately $600,000. Ferrari's 812 Competizione and its variants use a 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V-12 revving to 9,500 rpm — the closest thing to an old-school twelve still in production — though Ferrari has signaled the front-engined V-12 GT segment will eventually electrify. The Zenvo Aurora, a Danish hypercar confirmed for limited production and priced above €2.8 million, also uses a V-12, making it perhaps the most extreme remaining example. BMW's M760e, the top-tier 7 Series, pairs a 4.4-liter V-8 with a plug-in hybrid system — not a V-12 — so the brand no longer fields a twelve-cylinder production car in the current generation. No major automaker has publicly committed to a specific end date for V-12 production in the way some brands announced internal-combustion phase-outs broadly. But the trajectory is clear from what they have and haven't said. Lamborghini has confirmed the Revuelto's hybrid V-12 will carry the configuration forward for this generation, with no pure combustion successor planned. Ferrari has spoken about electrification across its lineup without specifying when the V-12 exits, though the company has emphasized it will preserve the engine's character as long as regulations allow. Rolls-Royce, which launched the all-electric Spectre in 2024, has positioned electrification as additive rather than immediately replacing the V-12 — but the long-term direction is not ambiguous. The Maybach S680's continued availability is perhaps the most accessible entry point into V-12 ownership for buyers who aren't in the Rolls-Royce or Lamborghini price bracket. At $240,000-plus it is hardly affordable, but it is the least expensive confirmed V-12 production car on the current market. Whether Mercedes-Benz extends the V-12 into the next S-Class generation remains unconfirmed. Given tightening European emissions standards and the brand's stated EQ electrification push, the current S680 may represent the final generation of the configuration in the sedan segment. The V-12 isn't gone yet — but the list of cars that offer one has never been shorter, and the manufacturers still building them are either hybridizing the format or staying quiet about how much longer they'll continue. Road & Track's S680 test is a reminder that the window to buy a new twelve-cylinder car is open, just not indefinitely. For buyers who care about the format, the time to act is now rather than when the last allocation is spoken for. We want to hear from you. title: The Wistar Institute Receives Grant from V Foundation for Cancer Research to Advance Melanoma Studies | Newswise - Newswise
content: Browse experts available to comment on breaking news Request an expert contact, get responses directly to your inbox Find an expert by topic in a comprehensive database Newswise — PHILADELPHIA — (WEDNESDAY, JULY 29, 2026) — The Wistar Institute, an international biomedical research leader in cancer, immunology, and infectious disease, has received an $800,000 translational grant from the V Foundation for Cancer Research. The grant, part of the V Foundation’s Breaking Barriers in Cancer Research Award program, will allow Jessie Villanueva, Ph.D., and her lab to pursue research into new potential ways to treat drug-resistant melanoma. Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, and cases continue to rise. While current treatments help many of those fighting melanoma, approximately 50% of patients do not respond to treatments. “This translational grant helps support our efforts to make targeted therapy and immunotherapy work better,” explains Villanueva, associate professor in the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program of the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center, and member, Melanoma Research Center, at The Wistar Institute,. “Our goal is to find treatments that either fully remove tumors or keep them away for as long as possible. By going after the cells that survive treatment, we hope to improve outcomes for people with melanoma.”Villanueva’s lab focuses on melanoma with mutations in the NRAS gene, a particularly aggressive and treatment-resistant form of cancer that is found in about one-fourth of patients. Until recently, there were few treatments for these tumors. Villanueva and her team have identified a key vulnerability in treatment resistant melanoma cells harboring mutations in NRAS—one that may be targeted by disrupting how these cells process fats and manage stress. By testing promising drug combinations, including some using existing FDA-approved therapies, the lab aims at stopping resistant cells earlier and help create longer-lasting responses for people with melanoma. “I’m truly thankful to the V Foundation for their support of this important project,” said Villanueva. “Although we focus on melanoma, this research has broader implications and some of our findings could also help improve treatment for other types of cancer driven by mutant RAS.” The V Foundation for Cancer Research was founded in 1993 by the late Jim Valvano, legendary North Carolina State University basketball coach, ESPN commentator and member of the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. The V Foundation has funded over $500 million in game-changing cancer research grants in North America through a competitive process strictly supervised by a world-class Scientific Advisory Committee. Because the V Foundation has an endowment to cover administrative expenses, 100% of direct donations are awarded to cancer research and programs. The V team is committed to funding the best scientists to accelerate a Victory Over Cancer and save lives. The Wistar Institute is the nation’s first independent nonprofit institution devoted exclusively to foundational biomedical research and training. Since 1972, the Institute has held National Cancer Institute (NCI)-designated Cancer Center status. Through a culture and commitment to biomedical collaboration and innovation, Wistar science leads to breakthrough early-stage discoveries and life science sector start-ups. Wistar scientists are dedicated to solving some of the world’s most challenging problems in the field of cancer and immunology, advancing human health through early-stage discovery and training the next generation of biomedical researchers. wistar.org. title: Amicus Brief: Clemente Properties v. Pierluisi-Urrutia - Manhattan Institute
content: Don't miss the newsletters from MI and City Journal Roberto Clemente’s sons and their companies have spent decades protecting the baseball legend’s name, image, and trademark. In 2021, however, Puerto Rico enacted laws requiring motorists to pay for license plates and registration tags bearing Clemente’s mark. The program generated roughly $15 million for a government fund, despite the family’s objections and without paying compensation. The Clementes sued under the Lanham Act—the federal trademark law—and the Fifth Amendment. The First Circuit allowed some trademark claims against individual officials to proceed but dismissed the takings claim, holding that the Supreme Court’s categorical—or per se—takings rules don’t apply to “intangible” property. It also held that Puerto Rico enjoys state-like sovereign immunity which the Lanham Act didn’t abrogate. Now on petition for Supreme Court review, the Manhattan Institute and the Instituto de Libertad Económica para Puerto Rico (the commonwealth’s free-market think tank) have filed an amicus brief supporting the Clementes. We argue that a trademark’s essential property right is the power to exclude unauthorized commercial use. When Puerto Rico placed the Clemente mark on government products, set a price, collected the money, and kept the proceeds, it appropriated that core right rather than merely regulating it. The First Circuit’s tangible-intangible distinction has no basis in the Fifth Amendment’s text, founding-era understandings, or longstanding precedent protecting franchises, patents, contracts, liens, and other incorporeal rights. It also threatens brands, trade secrets, data, goodwill, and other assets central to the modern economy. Although the brief takes no position on Puerto Rico’s ultimate immunity, it warns that the rulings below could leave owners with property rights that lack remedies when violated. The Court should hear the case and reaffirm that government must pay for what it takes—even when the property can’t be touched physically. title: Tested: The Gas-Powered 2026 Honda CR-V Has Good Vibes, but Is the Hybrid Better? - MotorTrend
content: Honda’s stalwart SUV is as good as you remember, but the hybrid version is arguably the better buy. We know why you’re here, so we won’t bury the lede: Yes, the Honda CR-V is, in just about every meaningful way, still the same cheerful compact SUV that has established itself as a go-to purchase over three decades and six generations. The 2026 Honda CR-V EX-L AWD tested here is the most well-equipped gas-only model, with a price that places it smack in the middle of the CR-V lineup, above the gasoline LX and EX and the least expensive hybrid, the Sport. We liked the CR-V EX-L a lot—but is it good enough to be your next daily driver? Can this gas-only iteration make a case for itself against its competition, not to mention the hybrid CR-V in the same showroom? Let’s dig in. We’ll start with the basics of the EX-L AWD. For $38,805 as tested, you get a 1.5-liter, 190-hp turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a CVT automatic, and optional AWD. Leather-trimmed seats, a power tailgate, parking sensors, low-speed braking capability, eight-speaker sound, and an auto-dimming rearview mirror round out the EX-L’s light-luxury features. It’s cheaper than the hybrid CR-V’s entry-level Sport trim, but only slightly, with their base MSRPs just a few hundred dollars apart. The CR-V lineup got a comprehensive redesign for the 2023 model year, which brought a refined shape and such niceties as 18-inch wheels and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto—but there’s not much you couldn’t get on, say, a decently optioned EX. Perhaps a look inward will reveal the EX-L’s value proposition. With its leather touches, the EX-L’s cabin is a bit nicer than lower-trim CR-Vs, but you won’t find yards of luxury materials or big infotainment screens here. Everything inside feels high quality, durable, and well assembled, though, and the 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen is perfectly adequate for tasks related to operating a motor vehicle and its basic functions. Its front-and-center placement on the dashboard keeps your head up and eyes in the general direction of the road, and its unique blend of hard buttons and touchscreen functionality works well. Likewise, the 10.2-inch driver display is, uh, somewhat spartan, with a couple of round, digitally rendered gauges and a small center readout for tracking things like cruise control status as its default state. It is customizable to a degree, but there’s just not enough room to change things up too much. We appreciate Honda’s resistance to unnecessarily large interfaces in the CR-V—in no small part, admittedly, because it necessitates old-school physical controls for basic functions like climate and audio, which we’re coming to regard as nonnegotiable. Honda Sensing, Honda’s suite of driver assists, is included in every CR-V. It provides pre-collision braking, throttle control, and steering functions, as well as lane keeping, adaptive cruise control with Traffic Jam Assist, adaptive headlights, parking sensors, and cross traffic monitoring, among many other features. We found the adaptive cruise and traffic jam functions especially useful, though several times we noted an uncomfortable abruptness to the system’s braking in traffic, which might make us think twice about using it a lot. We found nothing uncomfortable about the CR-V EX-L’s perforated-leather-trimmed seats, though. Both rows are roomy and supportive, with plenty of legroom for front and rear passengers. The EX-L gets four-way power front seats, and for 2026 both rows get charging capability, with a wireless phone charger, USB-A, and USB-C for the folks up front and two USB-C ports for the rear passengers. Cargo space is one place the gas-only CR-V may have the hybrids beat—because it doesn’t have the same drivetrain componentry to package, the gas variant enjoys 3 extra cubic feet behind the second row, for a total of 39.3. There’s plenty of cargo room with the rear seats up and quite a bit more when you fold them. With rear seats up or down, the CR-V EX-L’s cargo volume beats the Toyota RAV-4, Subaru Forester, and Nissan Rogue, too. Overall, the CR-V’s ergonomics and layout feel familiar, with controls that are thoughtfully laid out and excellent outward visibility—in short, all the things that make getting into a 2026 CR-V like slipping on an old sweater are in evidence. You’ll have to decide whether that’s a desirable quality or not. With a turbocharged, direct-injected 1.5-liter I-4 engine pushing 190 horsepower and 179 lb-ft of torque through a CVT automatic, the AWD CR-V EX-L went from 0 to 60 mph in 8.4 seconds in our testing, which makes it a tad slow for the broader segment. Notably, it’s also slower than it used to be. In 2026, the CR-V’s natural enemy, the Toyota RAV4, can get to 60 mph more than a second quicker at minimum, but with a big caveat to bear in mind: All RAV4s are now hybrids. A 2025 RAV4 with the now-retired gas powertrain needed around eight seconds, and the newly redesigned gas Mazda CX-5 needed 8.8 seconds to get to 60 mph in our testing. And the CR-V hybrid? It’s right on the RAV4, with a 0–60-mph time of about 7.5 seconds. All that being said, though, our gas CR-V didn’t feel especially slow. From a stop and when hitting the accelerator from low speeds, it exhibited little of the throttle lag or surging that often plagues vehicles with small turbocharged engines. It revs like a Honda should, but it does so linearly, smoothly, and without drama, in part thanks to its CVT transmission, which feels as much like a traditional automatic as you could reasonably expect. That’s only part of what makes the 2026 CR-V an unexpected pleasure to drive, though. Its brakes have surprisingly good feel for a vehicle of this kind, with decent bite and a pedal that accurately translates what’s going on at the wheels. Handling is similarly pleasing. The term “carlike” gets throw around a lot in regard to small SUVs, but in this case, it’s apt; the CR-V isn’t a canyon-carver, but we think its cornering, AWD grip, and general sense of composure and stability make it above average for the segment—even, dare we say, a little bit fun. Steering feel did leave something to be desired, though. Also leaving something to be desired is the gas CR-V’s fuel economy. We realized about 26 mpg average in our time with the SUV, good for a driving range in the neighborhood of 364 miles—significantly less than the official rating of 27/31/29 mpg city/highway/combined should yield. AWD doesn’t help matters, but as you’d expect, the hybrid variants trounce the gas CR-Vs in this regard, even when identically equipped—the most efficient AWD hybrid gets 40/34 mpg city/highway and 518 miles of range, and even the least efficient hybrid variant, the new TrailSport, gets 38/33 mpg and can go nearly 500 miles between fill-ups. If you’re thinking it sounds like the CR-V is behind the times, we can’t argue with you—but that may be one of its greatest selling points. It neither overwhelms nor underwhelms; it’s a totally familiar, even comforting experience while managing to offer some driver engagement. It’s easy to see what makes this vehicle the default for so many buyers, year after year. If you want the nicest gas-only 2026 CR-V you can get, you’ll find little to regret about the EX-L. If you’re looking for maximum value and the most traditional CR-V experience, though, the second-tier EX or even the base LX may offer enough for thousands less than the EX-L. And while we’re at it, unless you’re allergic to orange accents, we think the Sport Hybrid, which starts within a few hundred dollars of the EX-L but offers superior power and efficiency and comparable amenities, is worthy of serious consideration. Whatever flavor you choose, though, it’s tough to go wrong with a Honda CR-V. Get the newest car reviews, hottest auto news, and expert analysis of the latest trends delivered straight to your inbox! title: 2026 Honda CR-V EX-L vs. 2026 Mazda CX-5 Premium Plus Tested: Which Compact SUV Is Better? - Car and Driver
content:
The CX-5 and CR-V are both longtime Car and Driver favorites, but with the Mazda fully redesigned for 2026, which one comes out on top? Let's make a bet. Head over to your well-lit display case (or back closet) stacked full of old Car and Driver issues, dust off any 10Best issue from the last decade or so, and we'd wager that either the Honda CR-V or Mazda CX-5 is on that list. With nine of the 10 most recent 10Best lists containing either the Honda or the Mazda, it's clear that the two models are perennial favorites around our office—and, according to sales figures, around the country. Since Mazda gave the CX-5 a full redesign for 2026, we figured it was a good time to get these two longtime favorites together for a bit of friendly competition. Much like a Burger King order, the 2026 Honda CR-V can be had your way. The lineup starts with the LX at $32,370, which is powered by a 190-hp turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-four, and is available in front- or all-wheel drive. If you're looking for a bit more power, a few more features, or better fuel economy, the CR-V's got you covered with an entire lineup of hybrids. We tested a 2026 EX-L, the top trim for nonhybrid CR-Vs, starting at $36,850; the all-wheel drive and optional Radiant Red Metallic paint push its as-tested price to $38,805. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V for sale near 60629 Currently, Mazda's CX-5 stable contains just one powertrain, although a hybrid model is slated to arrive for 2027. Every 2026 CX-5, including our Premium Plus test model, comes equipped with a 187-hp 2.5-liter inline-four, and all-wheel drive is standard. The CX-5's price band is a bit broader than the Honda's, starting at $31,485 and rising all the way to $40,485, with our test example coming in at $41,080 with its extra-cost Aero Gray Metallic paint. Whether you see Honda's interior design as a positive or a negative is up to you, but the fact is, the design works. The CR-V's interior is roomy and easy to see out of. The materials—at least in our EX-L—are high-quality and comfortable to the touch even if they don't impress much beyond that. The layout is simple, with 9.0 inches of infotainment screen acreage to provide you with what you need, but not enough to overwhelm. Climate controls are fuss-free. Want it warmer? Turn that obviously placed dial on the dashboard to the right. Is your butt a little cold? Don't worry, the heated seat button is placed well within arm's reach. Can't quite hear the music over the sound of your own singing? You've got physical controls on the steering wheel and infotainment screen ready to pump up the volume. HIGHS: Smart interior layout, hugely practical, confidence-inspiring dynamics. LOWS: Noisy cabin, lacks any premium feel, could be quicker. VERDICT: Easy to love, hard to hate. Mazda's interior, on the other hand, goes all in on digital controls. The new-generation CX-5 places just about every non-driving function, from volume to vehicle settings, on the 15.6-inch dash-mounted do-it-all touchscreen. So long as you're cool with this approach, the CX-5's interior impresses. The seats, doors, and dashboard all sport leather wrappings, and the new "Mazda" script on the steering wheel evokes thoughts of luxury goods. Sitting in the CX-5, you're met with a cozy space that feels more premium than what's in the Honda, but we can't help noticing that the refreshed car doesn't seem quite as upscale as the older version. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V for sale near 60629 The CR-V's airy cabin puts a premium on passenger space and narrowly edges the CX-5 in rear-seat room—this despite the Honda having a shorter wheelbase: 106.3 inches to the Mazda's 110.8. In compact SUVs, storage space is as important as passenger comfort, and the CR-V wins there as well, offering 39 cubic feet behind the rear seats and 77 cubic feet with the seats folded. The CX-5 has 34 cubic feet behind the rear seats and only improves to 67 cubic feet with the rear seats laid flat. From an exterior-design perspective, we prefer the CX-5. Both models are reasonably handsome, but the Mazda's muscular lines and swoopy roofline evoke a bit more emotion, while the CR-V's aging design feels a tad more mundane. Should the two ever enter a drag race together, the result would be close. Despite the CX-5's extra 262 pounds, its 8.3-second run to 60 mph matches that of the lighter CR-V. The Mazda noses ahead in the quarter-mile, beating the Honda by 0.1 second, although the CR-V's 3-mph-higher trap speed shows the Honda is pulling harder by the end. That continues beyond the quarter-mile, where the CR-V reaches 100 mph 2.4 seconds sooner than the CX-5. Champagne for the winner, even if it is by the slimmest of margins. HIGHS: Superior ride quality, quieter cruising, more stylish looks. LOWS: "Everything's computer," ho-hum fuel economy, higher price. VERDICT: Still great but slips a little with this redesign. Honda did an admirable job tuning the CR-V's continuously variable automatic transmission to reduce that tech's worst attributes, but nothing beats the real thing, which is what you get in the Mazda. Urge the CX-5 to accelerate for a pass on the highway, and the six-speed automatic transmission kicks down to provide extra power for the task. And against the stopwatch, the Mazda beat the Honda in our 50-to-70-mph highway passing test by two-tenths. Despite that, the CR-V feels reasonably peppy. Give the throttle a good stab, and the Honda responds. Tell the CX-5 to accelerate, and it's got a hair more urgency than the CR-V, although the engine feels and sounds a bit less refined in doing so. The CR-V's small-displacement engine is efficient, earning EPA estimates of 27 mpg in the city and 31 mpg on the highway. That beats the CX-5's numbers, which are 24 mpg in the city and 30 mpg on the highway. Our test CR-V's observed fuel economy came in at 25 mpg; we don't yet have results for the CX-5 in that same test. At a steady 70 mph, the Mazda is noticeably quieter than the Honda. The former measures at just 23 sones, while the latter lets in more wind and road noise at 26 sones, or some 13 percent louder. However, the Mazda's coarse powertrain is more vocal under acceleration, measuring at 77 decibels to the Honda's 74 at wide-open throttle. Still, settle into a cruise on the highway, and either cabin becomes a quiet enough place to happily spend your commute. Leave your daily drive behind, and both cars are considerably more athletic than they need to be. The CR-V drives like most Hondas, with nicely weighted steering that has a solid on-center feel. The Honda has a touch more body roll than the Mazda, but unless you're driving them back to back, you'd be hard-pressed to notice the difference. The CX-5 is similarly dynamic. The steering has more of an artificial feel than the Honda's, but it provides confidence-inspiring feedback and a clear sense of on-center. We prefer the CX-5's softer ride to the CR-V's slightly stiffer one. Neither beats you up over bumps, but the Honda jolts you a bit more, especially over sharp impacts. The CR-V takes the crown thanks mostly to its easier-to-use interior, additional usable space, and its lower price. That's not to say the CX-5 isn't a contender. It's got solid dynamics, and it looks great—as long as you don't mind the screen-centric interior design. Furthermore, the Honda's more efficient powertrain and lower starting price make the CR-V the thriftier option up front and going forward. And in this segment, practicality counts.
